title: My daughter invited me to her company's awards dinner. When they announced the employee of the year, they put my photo on the screen — even though I'd never worked there (PART 2)

blocks.text: …The audience applauded again. I didn't move. Emily's grip on my hand was so tight it hurt.
"Mom," she whispered, "there's a release form in the gift bag they're going to hand you on stage. Do not sign it."
I didn't go up. The CEO waited, smiled, made a joke about my modesty and moved on. Emily walked me out through the kitchen while a jazz band started playing.
In the hotel parking garage, sitting in her car, my daughter told me what she'd discovered.

When Emily was born in 2004, I'd had an emergency C-section at a university hospital in Durham. Afterward, I'd been asked to sign a stack of forms, half-conscious, including one allowing "routine tissue samples" from the delivery to be used for research. I didn't remember it. Most women wouldn't.
A team of engineers and biologists at the hospital took cells from Emily's umbilical cord and my placenta and discovered they grew in a way no one had seen before.

They became the foundation of a stem-cell line the scientists called M-04. The engineers later spun off a company. It was now worth over three billion dollars. Its most successful products all traced back to M-04.

The photo of me with the engineers was real. They'd come to my room the day after Emily was born, introduced themselves as researchers, and asked to take a picture "for the department newsletter." I was exhausted and on painkillers, and I said yes. The name the CEO used, "Margaret Hale," was the code name they'd given the donor in their records.

Emily had applied to the company because she admired its work. A few weeks after she started, a senior scientist noticed her last name and her birth date, connected them, and quietly asked her to dinner. He told her that the company's lawyers were nervous.

New laws were coming on donor consent, and a lawsuit from the original donor could cost them billions. The awards dinner was their solution: a public thank-you, a plaque, a check for fifty thousand dollars, and a release form signed in front of hundreds of witnesses.
"They wanted you to sign away everything with a smile," Emily said.

I hired a lawyer the following week. She specialized in medical consent cases. After a year of negotiations, the company agreed to a settlement and an ongoing royalty on M-04 products. They also agreed to publicly credit the cell line's origin and to establish a fund for informed-consent education for new mothers.
Emily quit before the settlement was signed. She's in graduate school now, studying bioethics.

Last month, the senior scientist who'd warned her sent me an email with a photograph attached: a petri dish under a microscope, glowing faintly. The caption said, "You and Emily. Still helping people, twenty-two years later." It's the strangest baby picture I own, and one of my favorites.
